extracted.intended_audience: judges, criminalists, forensic psychologists, trial lawyers, and examiners of witness testimony
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating the reliability and probative value of witness statements, with attention to effects of intoxication, suggestion, and situational influences on memory and behavior in forensic and courtroom settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of intoxication and their behavioral/legal significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The text distinguishes stages: an early stage where irritability coexists with self-satisfaction and the drinker is still self-possessed; a next period where 'memory and understanding have quite left him' so he 'acts as if the present moment were the only one' and is 'much more dangerous to himself and others'; and a last period where the drunkard 'has so lost his senses that he has no more idea of his external environment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the stage to judge control and reliability: early-stage effects and outbreaks 'may be suppressed' and the drinker 'is not likely to lose control' unless excited; in the second stage the person rarely knows what he is doing and 'must be considered a pure fool'; in the last period the person is oblivious to environment. These distinctions bear on assessing responsibility, dangerousness, and testimonial reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of alcohol is an unreliable predictor of intoxication effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The author states 'the quantity of drink is indifferent' because alcohol effects are highly individual: 'there are young and powerful men who may become quite foolish on half a glass of wine... and there are weak old people who can carry unbelievable quantities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer impairment or reliability solely from the reported amount consumed. Instead, prefer knowledge of an individual's regular reaction to alcohol as a safer guide; be cautious drawing general rules about quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual factors and drinking method alter intoxication
rubrics_metrics.description: How a man drinks influences intoxication: 'a small quantity of wine can intoxicate if it is soaked up with bread which is repeatedly dipped into the wine.' Wine drunk in a cellar or while laughing, being merry, vexed, when a large variety of drinks is taken, or when taken on an empty stomach acts more strongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating impairment, consider drinking method, accompanying food, emotional state during drinking, mixing of drinks, and environment (e.g., cellar). These situational modifiers can intensify effects irrespective of quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcohol can produce selective/amnesic memory loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Alcohol's effect on memory is often selective: many people 'lose their memory only with respect to a single very narrow sphere' — e.g., remember everything except their names, residence, marital status, friends, or even their own identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to domain-specific amnesia in witnesses or defendants. Such selective memory failures may be believable when reported secondhand but are treated skeptically when asserted by the defendant in court; this affects credence and evidentiary evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion as a pervasive influence on testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestion is widespread and not limited to explicit suggestive questions: it includes 'the influence of the judge on the witnesses, the witnesses upon each other, the conditions upon the witnesses' and occurs 'through the stories of friends, through the examples of strangers, through our physical condition, through our food, through our small and large experiences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing testimony, account for subtle and pervasive suggestion sources (authority figures, co-witnesses, prior stories, environmental/physiological states). Treat suggestion as a broad determinant that can 'determine' responses without overt persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestive questioning: inevitability and limited harmless forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Older criminalists 'have rigorously limited the putting of suggestive questions,' yet some are unavoidable; Mittermaier observed many questions 'had to suggest their answers' (e.g., 'Has A said that... ?') and considered such questions often 'the most harmless.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between suggestive questions that are practically unavoidable and those that are prejudicial. Recognize that some leading or suggestive phrasings are necessary for fact-finding, but remain cautious about their potential to implant or shape witness recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-question sources of bias: public opinion, newspapers, experience, and fancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses, experts, and judges are 'subject, especially in great and important cases, to the influence of public opinion, of newspapers, of their own experiences, and finally, of their own fancies,' causing testimony and judgments 'less guided by the truth than by these influences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how media coverage, community sentiment, prior experiences, and imaginative preconceptions may have biased witnesses or decisionmakers. Such influences can contaminate independent recollection and expert opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertain and contested authority over assessing suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: The text notes the 'contradictory are the opinions concerning the determination of [suggestion's] value—whether it is to be determined by the physician or by the judge; and finally, how little we know about suggestion anyway.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge limits of current knowledge about suggestion. Avoid definitive attributions of suggestibility without careful observation and data collection; prefer empirical study and cautious interpretation rather than overconfident judgments by either physicians or judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against premature conclusions — prioritize observation and evidence gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite the extensive literature, 'we still have too little material, too few observations, and no scientifically certain inferences' about suggestion; the author recommends 'it is best to wait and to give our attention mainly to observation, study, and the collection of material.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should favor systematic observation, accumulation of case evidence, and empirical study over speculative assertions about suggestive influences. Use collected material to inform, not to overrule, cautious courtroom inferences.
